COMMENTS - Tunzelmann reported a number
of cases of acute poisoning from drinking water
containing lead.
In one such case, a cook was ill for three
weeks. Unable to retain any food in the stomach,
constant nausea and, even when no food was
taken, frequent vomiting of greenish watery fluid ,
worse at night.
Skin was yellowish, conjunctiva decidedly
yellow. Tongue was furred , coated at back, very
yellow, horrible taste, fetor of breath, bowels
confined. Extreme debility. Hydr. 3c gave great
relief, but three months later the hands became
paralyzed, which led to the testing of the drinking
water and the discovery of lead.
A boy, age 12, had bronchial catarrh with a
loose cough and consolidation of left apex. As
soon as the poisoned water was stopped, he
rapidly recovered.

Women who work with lead frequently
abort. Women who do not work with lead but

Plumbum metallicum
Frohling related the case of N., a farmer, 46,
who was taken ill in November 1893 with attacks
of colic with vomiting and extreme constipation,
action only obtained by large enemata. Had been
constipated in former years, but without illness.
Op. had given only temporary relief.
After December 1983, vomiting was rare ,
but colic increased in intensity up to February
1894, when Frohling saw him first and found
him wasted to a skeleton, abdomen drawn in,
appetite bad, feeling ill.
His mind was somewhat affected, unable to
give sensible answers to questions. Constant
urgent call to stool, but only small, hard, black
balls were passed. Liver dullness only heard
from upper border of sixth to upper border of
seventh rib.
Lead poisoning was suspected, but as no
evidence of it could be found, Plb. 6c three
times a day was prescribed. In six days the colic
attacks were less frequent and less severe, two
stools passed without enema, his mind clearer.
Improvement continued in all respects, and
in fourteen days N. was able to leave his bed to
which he had been confined since November. By
the middle of March he made an hour's journey
to see Frohling and was hardly recognizable ,
he had gained so much nesh and his liver was
of normal size.
Wingfield reported two characteristic cases.
The first concerned Mrs. D., 50, no children,
sparely built, very nervous, constipated fifteen
years, took a teaspoonful of Cascara extract
every other night. Tongue coated with yellowish
white fur. Had constant headaches and after each
motion was thoroughly exhausted and had to lie
down the rest of the day.
Plb. 6x was given, three grains twice a day. In
two days, bowels began acting naturally.
In three weeks the headaches were gone,
tongue clean, much less nervous.
Wingfield's second case was Miss M., 25,
florid, had boils appear on face and arms and
chronic constipation. The constipation had been
a trouble since she was twelve years old. Slight
spinal curvature. Tongue furred, occasional
headaches. Suffered much during menstrual
periods. Plb. 6x twice daily at once relieved the
constipation and soon the boils disappeared.
Patient soon felt quite well.

Theuerkauf cured a case of hypopion with

Skinner cured a case of epilepsy in which the

W. H. Woodyatt reported a case of "vasomotor neurosis" affecting the left eye. Mrs. D., 29,
had been ill for two weeks and supposed she
had caught cold in the eye. She had a drooping
upper lid, intense photophobia, very profuse
lachrymation of hot tears, peri-corneal injection,
deep bluish redness of sclerotica, most marked
at corneal margin. Cornea was very faintly hazy.
Pupil contracted. Sight misty.
Ars. 6x and Plant. 6x failed to relieve. Plb. 6x
was then given with immediate improvement.
which went on to cure in seven days.
Plb. cured a case of right-sided sciatica that
had been greatly benefited by Gnaph. 1c, but
which had returned. The symptoms included
stiffness, soreness from great trochanter and
point of exit of nerve to knee, weakness in thigh,
worse by stooping, walking causes sensation as
if pushing a knife in thigh.
Plb. 6c was given four times day. Up to the
twelfth day there was no change, on that day,
the pain suddenly disappeared. The case had
lasted nine months.

HERBAL· Podophyllum grows throughout the United
States in damp, shady places, usually in woods. It
has five to nine-lobed leaves, large white nodding
flowers, and yellowish, egg-shaped fruits. The
fruits are not unlike a small lemon, hence the plant
is sometimes called "wild lemon." It flowers in May
and June, and the fruit ripens in October.

HERBAL-The tenn Polygonatum,derives from Greek,
"poly" meaning "many" and "gony," "gonato" referring to "knee." Solomon's Seal is true to doctrine of
signatures as the "white roots appear to be bony,
joints, knuckles and vertebra."
In AD. 130-200, the most famous physicians
of the day, Galen, Dioscorides, and Pliny all
recommended the use of Solomon's Seal root for
blemishes, bone repair, joint restoration, feminine
health, and as a heart tonic.
The herbalist,John Gerard,in his Herball,claimed
that it was effective for cuts, wounds and bruises of
all kinds. He claimed the roots were excellent for
"broken bones to knit."
Polyg-m., in material doses of tincture or low
potencies, has been found useful in treating all
kinds of musculoskeletal disorders.
Astringent, demulcent and tonic. Combined
with other remedies, Solomon's Seal is given tn
pulmonary consumption and bleeding of the
lungs. It is useful also in female complaints.
Solomon's seal has been used in the form of
a poultice and is believed to prevent excessive
bruising and to stimulate tissue repair.
The infusion of 1 oz. to a pint of boiling water
is taken in wineglassful doses and is also used
as an injection. It is a mucilaginous tonic, very
healing and restorative, and is good in inflammations of the stomach and bowels, piles, and
chronic dysentery.
Adistilled water made from the whole plant has
been used as a skin tonic and is an ingredient
of expensive cosmetics.
COMMENTS-Rootcan be cooked. The root should
be macerated for some time in water in order
to remove bitter substances. Rich in starch.
Nonnally only used in times of famine, the root
was powdered and then made into a bread by
the Native Americans.
Young shoots can be cooked, boiled and used
as an asparagus substitute, they make an excellent vegetable and are widely used in Turkey.

PROGESTERONE
PHARMACY- prog. Progesterone. Planets: Moon.
Historical dose: All potencies.
CLINICAL- Acne. Amenorrhea. Bloating. Breast,
disorders. Constipation. Cramps. Depression.
Edema. Endometriosis. Epilepsy. Fatigue. Hair.

Insomnia. Menopausal, disorders. Menstrual,
disorders. Migraine. Miscarriage. Nausea. Obesity. Osteoporosis. Premenstrual syndrome.
Vaginal, dryness.
HOMEOPATHIC - Progesterone is a hormone
secreted by the ovary in the second two weeks
of the menstrual cycle in reproductive age ovulating women. Progesterone. or progesterone-like
substances called progestogens or progestins,
are ingested by women in birth control pills and
menopausal hormone replacement therapy.
Progesterone acts to stabilize the tissue lining
of the uterus (endometrium) so if it is absent,
such as with ovarian anovulation, irregular and
heavy menstrual bleeding often occurs after
a period without any menstrual bleeding. Thus
progesterone is used to prevent this irregularity
of bleeding if it is given continuously.
If, on the other hand, a onetime bolus of progesterone is given, then the falling progesterone
levels will actually cause an estrogen-primed
endometrium to slough and therefore start a
menses.
It is sometimes used to induce a menstrual
period or regulate abnormal bleeding problems
if menses are skipping or bleeding is irregular
or prolonged. Progesterone has been used as
therapy for premenstrual syndrome and for
women with infertility or frequent miscarriages .

Too much progesterone often causes tiredness and even sedation. This side effect can be
beneficial in a women who has epilepsy or even
uterine irritability causing preterrn labor because
progesterone in high doses can decrease seizure
activity and uterine contractions.
Progesterone tends to vaginal dryness by
counteracting the effect on lubrication of estrogens, and it can also decrease the amount of
menstruation or block it entirely by reversing
estrogen effect on the growth ofthe uterine lining.

Take it inwardly in syrups for inward wounds,
outwardly in unguents and plasters for outward.
The juice thereof used with oil of roses to annoint

remove headache."

j Prunus virginiana

virginiana has been used from time immemorial

HOMEOPATHIC-Prun-v. is a heart tonic. It relieves

heart, dilatation of right heart. Cough, worse at
night on lying down. Chronic bronchitis. Weak
digestion,especially in elderly people.lncreases
muscular tone.
Hale noted it for cough, sympathetic with heart

feeling in head" like that of the other Pruneae.
COMMENTS - Seymour Taylor said it is especially
useful in dilatation of right heart, whether as a
result of chronic bronchitis or of mitral stenosis.
Burnett used it for weak digestion especially
of elderly people. He regarded it as a mild form
of Hydr-ac.
Laidlaw gave as a particular indication persistent coughs acquired in winter, worse at night on
lying down. Spasmodic and asthmatic coughs.
Attacks of wheezing and whistling in trachea
and large bronchi and cough left behind after
an attack of influenza.
Laidlaw's first case was a delicate girl, 20,
who took cold, which began with coryza and
in a few days passed into a cough with scanty
expectoration and soreness under the sternum.
Cough was persistent and annoying at all times,
but worse at night.
After many other remedies had failed, Prun.,
one grain every two hours, relieved in two days
and cured in a week. A recurrence some months
later was rapidly cured by the same remedy.
REFERENCES- Boericke. Clarke.

PULMONARIA OFFICJNALIS

PHARMACY - pulm-v. Pulmo vulpis. Fox's lung.
Sarcode. Trituration. Planets: Moon. Historical
dose: All potencies.
CLINICAL -Asthma. Bronchitis. Dyspnea. Catarrh.
Heart, disease. Lungs, catarrh. Lungs, edema.

PHARMACY - pul-o. Pulmonaria officinalis. Lungwort. Pulmonaria maculosa. Jerusalem sage. N.
0. Boraginaceae. Planets: Merrury. Historical
dose: Tincture and all potencies.
CLINICAL-Asthma. Bronchitis. Coughs. Hemoptysis. Hemorrhoids. Lung, disorders. Urinary,
incontinence. Tuberculosis.
HERBAL - Pulmonaria officinalis is an evergreen
perennial species oflungwort, native to locations
throughout Europe. A rhizome, P. officinalis
produces small bunches of pink flowers which
turn to blue-purple in spring.
The plant has been cultivated for centuries as
a medicinal herb, the ovate spotted leaves were
thought to be symbolic of diseased lungs. The
appearance of the plant makes it easy to see
why the lungwort was used for diseases of the
lung (putrid bronchitis, hemoptysis), and also for
hematuria, and urinary incontinence.
The medicines are prepared from the fresh,
flowering herb. It is an astringent, demulcent,
diaphoretic, diuretic, emollient, expectorant,
ophthalmic, and resolvent.
· The leaves and flowering shoots are often used
for their healing effect in pulmonary complaints.
The leaves can also be used externally to stop
bleeding. They are harvested in the spring and
dried for later use. A distilled water made from
the plant is an effective eyewash for tired eyes.
The tannins in lungwort have a slight astringent
effect when applied to the skin, thereby reducing
secretions, relievin·g irritation, and improving
tissue firmness.
It has been used as a wash, poultice, or soak
for hemorrhoids and minor skin injuries such as
scrapes and sunburn.
Lungwort has a high mucilage content and
this makes it useful in the treatment of chest
conditions, being of particular benefit in cases of
chronic bronchitis.The herb is very mucilaginous
and contains silica, tannins and saponins. It
combines well with other herbs such as coltsfoot
(Tus-fa.) in the treatment of chronic coughs including whooping cough and can also be taken
to treat asthma.

Shortness of breath.

HOMEOPATHIC- The uses of tissues and organs
as remedies have thrown light on many curiosities of ancient medicine. As the fox is probably
the longest-winded of all animals, the doctrine of
signatures pointed to his lungs as a likely remedy for
short breath. Pulm-v. has persistent shortness
of breath, causing a attack of asthma on the
slightest motion. Strong,sonorous bubbling rales.
COMMENTS - Grauvogl put on record his case
of a women, 65, much reduced in flesh by a
persistent condition of humid asthma. It commenced with chronic catarrh and symptoms of
edema of the lungs.
Strong, sonorous bubbling, rattling, whistling sounds over whole chest and at some

distance away, perceptible also to hand laid
on chest. Accelerated shortness of breath
amounting to suffocation, even without corresponding heaving of the chest, frequently with
cough and inability to expectorate.
Sometimes in light cases, there is no catarrh
present and only persistent shortness of breath,
becoming a paroxysm of asthma on the least
bodily exertion. The patient could only live
sitting up, bent forward, constant lividity of
face, lips and limbs and dropsy of legs.
Heart's pulsations irregular and death seemed
imminent. Pulm-v. 1x grains right was given and
repeated in an hour. Visible improvement set in
but without increased expectoration. After a third
powder the patient was able to lie down and fell
into a refreshing sleep lasting several hours. In
eight days she engaged in her domestic duties.
REFERENCES - Clarke.

Bojanus related two cases, the first in which a
girl, 18, of good constitution with no hereditary
predisposition. had amenorrhea for six months
and a fit occurred at the time each period was
due. In the epileptic aura, she looked sad, pale
as death, had chewing movements.
Puis. 6c one dose a day was given. The next
month, menses returned and there were no
more fits.
The second case was of a robust girl, 14,
with no hereditary predisposition. She had fits
for twelve months. The exciting cause was the
non-appearance of menses. She had one great
fit per month, small fits daily. In the epileptic aura
she was self willed, angry, stood on one spot,
stared into vacancy, stamped her foot. In the fit
she cried. had deathly paleness, bit her tongue,
urine flowed. She continued the occupation she
was engaged with at the beginning of the fit. Puis.
30c one dose a day was given.
Some weeks after, she had a slight fit. Amonth
later, menses came on for first time, she had no
great fits, and small ones were rare. She was
given Puis. 30c one dose a week. A month later,
she had a great fit. Puis. was then given once a
day. She had no more great fits, only a few small
ones. The cure was ermanent.

HERBAL - Pyrethrum has bitter tonic properties like
those of chamomile (Anthemis nobilis) and is a
popular remedy in slight fevers, hence the name
"feverfew."
The Treasury of Botany noted that the smell of
the whole herb is said to be particularly offensive
to bees. Some popular insect powders were
made of the dried fiowers of Pyrethrum roseum.
Radix pyrethri, or Pellitory of Spain, which is
used as an irritant and as a toothache cure is
the root of Anachycles pyrethrum. The roots of
the genus have a hot taste, the source of the
name pyrethrum (fire).
HOMEOPATHIC - One observation was recorded
with pyrethrum; a boy, 3 1/2 took 50 minims of
the tincture. It nearly proved fatal, causing diarrhea, convulsions of a tetanic nature, twitchings,
loquacious delirium, restless, rapid and weak
pulse and profuse sweat at night.
Twitching of muscles, of limbs, subsided by
morning of third day.
Violent convulsions lasting an hour and leaving
the child apparently moribund, but he gradually
recovered.

COMMENTS - Drysdale prepared a tincture of
Pyrog.. which he preferred to call Pyrexin since ~t
is not a mere fever-producer. Others have called 11
Sepsin. but this is too close to Septicemia, aname
given to a related and perhaps identical nosode.
The provings and most of the clinical experi·
ence have been obtained from this preparation.
Subsequently, Dr. Swan potentized some septic
pus, which has also been proved and clinically
applied. There does not seem to be any marked
difference in their effects.
As Drysdale put it, "The most summary indica·
tion for Pyrog. would be to term it the Aconite of
the typhus or typhoid quality of pyrexia,· and it is
likely useful wherever there is poisoning by bacte·
rial products (e.g. in the hectic of tuberculosis).
Sepsis is the essence of its action.
H. C. Allen, who published the proving and most
of the cases in Med.Adv.. rightly describes Pyrog.
as a "Product of Sepsis." He gave the indication
for its use in septic state, "When the best selected
remedies fail to relieve or permanently improve,'
analogous to the action of Psor. and Sulph. in
other conditions.
Drysdale's original cases include a number in
which threatened typhoid was averted, a case of
tabes mesenterica cured, and one of ulceration
of the colon greatly benefited. Drysdale'ssuccess
was encouraging, but as he continued to use the
tincture and the lowest potencies it was difficult
to ke~p the preparation.

The remedy did not come into extensive
use until Burnett published his pamphlet on
Pyrogenium in Fevers and Blood-poisoning in
1888. Burnett used chiefly the 6c dilution, which
is perfectly harmless and which will keep indefinitely. Heath, who made one of the preparations
used by Burnett, gave some of it to Swan of New
York, who ran it up into the high infinitesimal.
Much of the American experience is with
Swan's potencies, including a proving by Sherbino. Yingling collected symptoms from many
reported cases and arranged them with the
symptoms of the proving.
In Sherbino's proving, hewascured incidentally
of a consciousness of the heart, and its working
and palpitation from least excitement or anxiety,
worse beginning to move, congestion to head as
if a stroke would ensue. Cact. had done no good.
Sherbino cured a case of puerperal fever with
Pyrog., being led to its selection by the very high
pulse rate. He also had a case of relapsed typhoid,
with pulse 140, temperature 102 F., both were
normal in twenty-four hours.
He had a third case of a young woman, 17, with
a fever and aching bones where the bed felt very
hard. She had a numb, paralytic feeling. As the
fever left, the pulse kept mounting up. Sherbino
used Swan's potency, Pyrog. 1OO,OOOc,repeated
as often as effect ceased.
Clarke had ample opportunity to observe the
power of Pyrog. over typhoid fever, typhoid, and
hectic states, including one of discharging abscess connected with Pott's disease of the spine.
Burnett had cases of fully developed typhoid
cut short at the height by Pyrog. 6c given every
two hours. In his pamphlet he included Dr.
Shouldham's successful experience with Pyrog.
6c in two cases of diphtheria sore throat.
Burnett also recorded that Pyrog. 5c, five
drops in water night and morning, assisted in the
cure of a case of anal fistula. Under its action
a sweating at the seat, which the man had for
many years, disappeared.The skin of his hands,
which were subject to dry eczema, assumed a
much cleaner aspect.
J. S. Hunt reported five cases of varicose
ulcers, all of which healed quickly under Pyrog.

HOMEOPATHIC-Pure radium is a white metal which
"oxidizes in water,bums paper,turns black on exposure to air and has the property of adhering finmly
to iron." This last quality is not without significance
and shows a close affinity with ferrum. It is found
in ore pitchblende.
The discovery of radium and its properties in
1898 by Pierre and Marie Curie set many persons
thinking and among them, naturally, those who
are engaged in the healing of the sick. Curie
himself made the first "proving."
He put a tiny bit of radium salt in an India rubber capsule and fastened it to his arm, leaving it
there for ten hours. When he took it off the skin
was red, the place turned into a wound, which
took four months to heal, leaving a white scar
the size of a shilling surrounded by discolored,
puckered skin.
On another occasion he left it for half an hour.
A wound appeared at the end of a fortnight and
took another fortnight to heal. On a third occasion, it was left for eight minutes only, two months
later the skin became red and a bit sore, but it
soon passed off.

RADON
(Radioactive Gas)
PHARMACY - rado. Radon. Radioactive gas.
Planets: Satum. Historical dose: All potencies.
CLINICAL - Adenocarci noma. Emphysema.
Lung cancer. Lung, disorders. Pneumonia,
interstitial. Pulmonary fibrosis. Respiratory lesions. Silicosis.
HOMEOPATHIC - Radon is a toxic radioactive
gas, formed by the natural radioactive decay of
uranium in rock, soil, and water. It is colorless,
odorless, tasteless, and chemically inert.
Radon gas decays into radioactive particles
that can get trapped in the lungs when breathed
in. The primary adverse health effect associated
with chronic exposure to radon is lung cancer.
Squamous cell carcinoma.Small cell carcinoma.
Large cell carcinoma. Adenocarcinoma.
Other harmful respiratory effects associated
with chronic exposure to radon include emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, respiratory lesions.
Chronic interstitial pneumonia. Silicosis.
COMMENTS - Uranium changes to different elements as it decays down to its final element of
lead.All of the elements it changes into are solids
except one, radon, which floats freely in the soil
and is easily drawn into the lower level of homes
by the natural flow of air.

R

Radon

Radon's primary hazard is caused from inhalation of the gas and its highly radioactive heavy
metallic decay products (polonium, lead, and
bismuth) which tend to collect on dust in the air.
REFERENCES - Murphy.

PHARMACY - ran-fi. Ranunculus ficaria. Lesser

Historical dose: All potencies.
CLINICAL - Hemorrhoids.
HERBAL - The "lesser celandine" is not botanically
related to the true celandine, Chelidonium majus,
or to the Figwort tribe (Scrophularia) although it is
named Scrophularia minor in old books.
Ran-fi. is in all respects a true crowfoot except that it has three deciduous instead of five
persistent sepals and nine petals instead of five.
Gerarde noted that "It growth in meadows, by
ditches and trenches and it is common everywhere in moist and dark places.
It comes forth about the Calends of March and
flower a little after: it beginneth to fade away in
April, it is quite gone in May afterwards it is hard
to be found, yea scarcely the root."
Gerarde wrote that the idea of its use in hemorrhoids was derived from the cluster of small
tubers growing around the crown of the root,
which bear a striking resemblance to a bunch
of hemorrhoids.
REFERENCES- Clarke.

CLINICAL. Anus, fissures. Breas~ fissures. Breast

HERBAL - Ratanhia is remarkable for its entire ,
ovate, acuminate leaves, covered on both sides
with silky hair; it is one of the species most known
as yielding the Rhatany root of commerce. All
the species of Krameria, as far as known, are
intensely astringent. The root of several species
of Krameria,especially Krameria triandra,is used
to make the remedy.
The Treasury of Botany noted that the infusion
of the root is blood-red, and has a history of being used to adulterate port wine. The Infusion
has been used as a gargle and wash , and the
powder, mixed with charcoal, forms an excellent
tooth-powder.
In Peru, an extract is made that is a mild,
easily assimilated astringent medicine, useful
for passive, bloody or mucus discharges. As a
tonic, it is used for the weakness of digestive
organs and muscular debility, and restores tone
to relaxed parts.
Ratanhia is useful for delicate and nervous
women , and to prevent miscarriage in those with
a history of it. Can arrest passive hemorrhages.
Styptic action, astringent. Used in intermittent
and putrid fevers.
HOMEOPATHIC-Teste put Rat. in his Sulph. group.
He wrote, of its pre-homeopathic use, "There is
perhaps no plant the properties of which have
been so well indicated by chance as this."

HERBAL - Rauwolfia serpentina, found in Java
and India, belongs to the Apocynaceae family. A
very old drug in Ayurvedic medicine, the roots
and rhizomes contain hypotensive and neurodepressive alkaloids.
In 1952, the Russian chemist Muller isolated
the specialized reserpine under the name of
"serpasil." Most of the alkaloids are built on the
base of reserpine, a harmonic group linked with
a second isoquinoleic group.
HOMEOPATHIC - The homeopathic proving was

was carried out on twenty-four doctors, using the
1x and 3x potencies, for a period of fourteen to
twenty-eight days.
W. Lee Templeton also conducted a proving at
the Facuity of Homeopathy in London in 1954-55
on six provers. using the 3x, 6x, 12c, and 30c
potencies, depending on the subject, fora period
of six months.
Beja of Orleans began a self-proving in
July-August 1956 using the 3x potency, for one
month, at the rate of 10 drops four times a day.
Finally, Julian undertook detailed clinical studies
to determine the range of action of Rauw. in a
homeopathic potency.

HERBAL -Rhodiola root has a legendary history dating back thousands of years. In 77 AD., the Greek
physician Dioscorides documented the medical
applications of the plant, which he then called redia
riza, in his classic medical text De Materia Medica.
Rhodiola rosea is a remarkable herb that has
a wide and varied history of uses. It is thought to
strengthen the nervous system, fight depression,
enhance immunity, elevate the capacityforexercise,
enhance memory, aid weight reduction, increase
sexual funclion and improve energy levels.lt has
long been known as a potent adaptogen.
Rhodiola rosea may be effective for improving
mood and alleviating depression. Pilot studies on
human subjects showed it improves physical and
mental performance, and may reduce fatigue.
Adaptogen tonic. Antioxidants. Anti-depressant
Adaptogen - Rhodiola rosea has long been
known as a potent adaptogen. Adaptogens
are natural plant substances that increase the
body's non-specific resistance and nonnalize
the functions of the body. It is believed that
adaptogens work by increasing the ability of cells
to manufacture and use cell fuel more efficiently.
Antioxidant - A range of antioxidant com·
pounds have been identified in Rhodiola and
significant free-radical scavenging activity has
been demonstrated for alcohol and water extracts
of Rhodiola.
Blood, sugar- The use of Rhodiola has been
found including its ability to regulate blood sugar
levels for diabetics and protect the liver from
environmental toxins.

Rhodiola root
Cancer. Rhodiola has been shown to increase
anti-tumor activity by increasing the body's
resistance to toxins. According to research the
oral administration of Rhodiola inhibited tumor
growths and decreased metastasis. It improved
urinary tissue and immunity in patients with bladder cancer. In other experiments with various
types of cancer, including adenocarcinomas, the
use of Rhodiola resulted in significant increased
survival rate.
Depression -Extracts of rhodiola, seem to
enhance the transport of serotonin precursors,
tryptophan, and 5-hydroxytryptophan into the
brain. When balanced, it imparts a a sense of
contentment and mental ease. Either too much
or too little serotonin on the other hand has been
linked to various abnormal mental states such
as depression.
Glands • It can also clinically enhance thyroid function without causing hyperthyroidism,
enhance thymus gland function and protect or
delay involution that occurs with aging. It can
also improve your adrenal gland reserves without
causing hypertrophy.
Hearing • Rhodiola has been known for its
ability to improve hearing .
Heart · Rhodiola thus regulates the heart beat
and counteracts heart arrhythmias. Rhodiola
has been found to decrease harmful blood lipids
and thus decrease the risk of heart disease. It
assists in the uptake of intracellular calcium into
the heart thus promoting a greater potential for
heart muscle contraction.
Immunity • Rhodiola both stimulates and
protects the immune system by reinstating
homeostasis (metabolic balance) in the body. It
also increases the natural killer cells (NK) in the
stomach and spleen. This action may be due to
its ability to normalize hormones by modulating
the release of glucocorticoid into the body.
Memory • Studies using proofreading
tests have demonstrated that Rhodiola rosea
enhances memorization and concentration
ability over prolonged periods. It increases the
bioelectrical activity of the brain which improves
memory and brain energy.

HERBAL-The golden flowered rhododendron grows
among the fog and storms of the Siberian mountains. It is not well known in general medicine, but
the Treasury of Botany said that "it is narcotic in ~s
properties and is used medicinally."
Gmelin, during his travels in Siberia, noted
that the Cossacks and Mongolians used it for
rheumatism and gout. The hunters and mountain
rangers would drink an infusion of it to remove
the weariness and pains from their limbs after
fatiguing expeditions.
Gmelin was the first to recommend rhododendron in Europe as a remedy for gout and
rheumatism.
The first publication on the subject was by
Professor Kolpin, of Stettin, in 1779. It was used
with greater or less success, and recommended
accordingly·by many German physicians.
HOMEOPATHIC - Rhod. is a gouty, rheumatic
remedy, affecting the fibrous tissues,forearm,
lower legs, small joints, bones, genitals, nerves,
and single parts. Fibrositis. Arthritis. Great weakness after slight exertion. Formication with sweat.
Undulating sensation. Tearing, zigzag, boring,
rapidly changing, descending, paralytic pains.

COMMENTS - Rhus-r. has almost identical action
as Rhus-t.; characteristic burning in the tongue,
tip feels sore. Pains are often one-sided and in
various parts, often remote and successive.
Pronounced yearly aggravation (Lach.).
H. C. Allen noted a periodicity in Rhus-r. that
marks it as a great anti-psoric. It is, he said, on
deeply psoric or tubercular constitutions that its
toxic effects are most felt and longest lasting."
Guernsey considered Rhus-r. deeper acting
than Rhus-t., being indicated in phlegmonous
erysipelas, especially where it begins in ankles
and moves gradually up the leg, moving in the
deeper tissues, with no fever, and for axillary
glands when the swelling is very deep and hard.
Millspaugh summarized the effects of Rhus
poisoning: the majority of poisonings have been
caused by Rhus-r., as first redness and swelling
of the affected part with intolerable itching and
burning, nowed by vertigo, weariness and a sort
of intoxication.
Farrington gave. as distinctive indications for
Rhus-r., an occipital headache with rheumatic
~tiffness of the nape. Drawing, tearing pains
1n legs. Pleurodynia when the pains shoot into
the shoulders.
Mahony reported a case of eczema on the
perineum and scrotum with sweat in cleft of
buttocks, both relieved in a week with Rhus-r.,
12c, twice daily.

HERBAL - Poison ivy grows in thickets and low
grounds in North America, flowering in June. It
was introduced into England as a plant in 1640.
In 1798, Dufresnoy of Valenciennes first used it
as a medicine.
It was brought to his notice by the cure of a
young man of a herpetic eruption (darter) of
six years duration, through his being accidentally poisoned with the plant. Dufresnoy used
it successfully in eruptive diseases, paralysis,
rheumatism and amaurosis.

1737

Rhus toxicodendron
A peculiarity of the plant is that it is more
poisonous during the night, and when bursting
into leaf, or at any time in June or July when
the sun is not shining upon it. The absence of
sunlight together with dampness, seems to favor
the exhalation of toxicodendric acid.
"An acrimonious vapor, combined with carburetted hydrogen, exhales from a growing
plant of the Poison Oak during the night. It can
be collected in a jar and is capable of innaming
and blistering the skin of persons of excitable
constitution who plunge their arms into it."
Though it is not certain that Hahnemann used
Rhus-1. at all or exclusively, Jahr gave a separate
presentation of the Rhus radicans symptoms.Under
the name of Rhus, Hahnemann published his proving of "Rhus radicans, also called Toxicodendron."
Botanists agree in recognizing no distinction
other than that of habit between the two.
The milky juice, which turns black on exposure,
is used as a marking ink (like Anac.), and as an
ingredient in varnishes for finishing boots.

Millspaugh noted several instances of rhus

among which the poison vine predominated;
only four escaped without symptoms. "Most of
the men soon began to show signs of being tired
and at the end of the fourth day six of them were
flat on their backs too sick for anything."
Actual contact with the plant is not necessary
in order to produce its effect. One such instance
occurred on a sultry day in June.Ayoung woman
drove a croquet ball across a lawn to a clump
of poison ivy that grew beside it. Knowing her
susceptibility, she reached under the plant and
drew out the ball without touching a leaf.
In the evening of the same day her face began
to itch and bum. That night her face swelled so
badly that the eyes were not merely closed, but
the lashes even disappeared in the swelling. It
took nearl two weeks for her to recover.

Generally, there is infiltration of the face and
eyes, and agglutination of the lids after sleep.
Great restlessness, pain, thirst and fever. The
surface of the skin becomes studded with confluent bullae where the cellular tissue is loose.
Then a dermatitis follows, resembling erysipelas; this may spread rapidly and finally be
communicated to the mucus membranes.
This is followed by swelling of the mouth and
throat, cough, nausea and vomiting.
Rheumatoid pains develop about the joints
and a painful stiffness asserts itself in the lumbar
region while the legs and arms become numb.
Confusion of mind and delirium may then set
in, during which the patient may become so
ill-humored, restless and anxious that he will
jump out of bed.
Concomitants include inflammation of the eyes.
dilation of the pupils, weak vision, and sometimes
diplopia. Nosebleed, brown-coated tongue with
triangular red tip. Swelling of parotids, difficult
swallowing. Griping, diarrhea, profuse urination.
Oppression, rapid pulse, prostration, soreness of
muscles, worse by exercise, bleariness, chilliness
followed by fever and copious sweat.
Neidhard added a note which brought out a
modification of "worse by rest," which is of the
greatest practical importance. Neidhard said that
the disease in which he had made the most use
of Rhus-!. is a form of rheumatism common in
North America and characterized by the following symptoms:
"Rigidity, paralytic weakness of the joints with
stinging pain along the tendons and muscles.
Swelling and redness on or near the joints.
Rheumatism of the hip joint and wrist seem to be
most effectually controlled by its action.
The greatest rigidity and pain is experienced
on first moving the joints after rest and on waking
up in the morning. After the joints are moved for
a while the pain is lessened."
Nash noted that the restlessness of Rhus-!.
will be found to qualify the symptoms in a large
proportion of the cases in which it will be called
for. It is as restless as Aeon. and Ars., but in a
different way from either. With Rhus-t. it is due
to the pain and soreness. temporarily better by
movement or a nervous internal uneasiness
which makes the patient want to be on the move
when there is no particular pain present.

Rhus toxicoclendron
Conditions can often change from Rhus-t. to
Bry., as well as the reverse. Hahnemann wrote
about "these two antagonistic sister remedies."
Each in its place successfully met with typhus
which prevailed in the countries desolated by the
war which raged from the summer of 1813 and
onwards. Of 183 cases treated by Hahnemann
in Leipzig, not one died.
Hahnemann perceived the keynote of the
Rhus-t. symptoms: "We observe," he said in his
preface to the proving, "this curious action, the
severest symptoms and sufferings are excited
when the body or the limb is at rest and kept as
much as possible without movement.
"The opposite of this, namely, an increase of
the symptoms by movement in much more rarely
observed." He contrasted Rhus-t. with Bry., which
has almost the same rheumatic pains but with
opposite modalities.
Hahnemann pointed out another keynote of
Rhus-t.: "Multiplied experience has taught me
that Rhus-t. is the most efficacious and the
specific remedy for the frequently fatal effects of
over~lifting inordinate exertions of the muscles
and contusions." He might have been led to this
inference by the "bruised and sprain-like pains"
and "stiffness" of the provings. Rhus-t. is in the
front rank of vulneraries.

RICINUS COMMUNIS
(Castor Oil)
PHARMACY -ric.Ricinus communis.Castor oil bean.
Palma christi. N. 0 . Euphorbiaceae. Tincture made
with hot alcohol and water.Trituration of fresh seeds.
Tincture of fresh plant. Planets: Moon, Saturn.
Historical dose: All potencies.
CLINICAL- Albuminuria. Aphthae. Arthritis. Breast,
disorders. Breast-feeding. Cholera. Cholera
infantum. Colic. Constipation. Diarrhea. Duodenum, catarrh. Dysentery. Eruptions. Gangrene.
Gastro-enteritis. Injury. Jaundice. Muscle pain.
Peritonitis. Sprains.
HERBAL- The castor oil plant is a native of Egypt
and India. In the tropics, it is a small tree growing to the height of eight or ten feet. It can be
cultivated as an annual, its stems reaching from
three to five feet.
Castor oil, obtained from the seeds, can
be rubbed into muscles and joints. Castor oil
packs, warm oil-soaked flannel, can be applied
to inflamed tissues or organs. Leaves can be
applied topically.
The blandest form in common use is "cold
drawn." i.e., expressed without the aid of heat
and contains the smallest amount of the acrid
principle. A decoction of the seeds, used in the
East and West Indies, contains a much larger
proportion. ·
Ric. has great power over breast-feeding. 0 .
McWilliams observed in the Cape Verde Islands
that the leaves of the plant were applied to the
breasts to increase the flow of milk if it were
delayed and even to produce it in women who
had never borne children or not suckled for years.
In increasing the flow of milk in nursing women,
the breasts were fomented with a decoction of
the leaves of the plant, the boiled leaves being
afterwards thinly spread on the breasts.
For producing milk in others more vigorous
measures were resorted to. The women had to
sit over a boiling decoction of the leaves, care
being taken to prevent the escape of steam.When
the decoction was sufficiently cool the parts were
bathed with it, and also the breasts to which the
leaves were applied as in the other case.

Ricinus communis
Women with well-developed breasts were
more easily influenced. When the breasts were
small and shriveled this treatment acted more
on the uterine system, bringing on the menses
long before their time or causing immediate flow
if the time is near.
HOMEOPATHIC - Hale made the first collection of
the pathogenetic effects of Ric. and pointed out
its analogy to cholera, which Salzer confirmed.
Cases of poisoning, some of them fatal, have
been recorded from the ordinary oil, but the
greater number of the pathogenetic effects have
resulted from eating the seeds.
Fatal effects have followed eating three seeds,
and one seed has caused violent effects. After
twenty seeds,gastroenteritisand death preceded
by general convulsions and collapse occurred.
Ric. has marked action on gastro-intestinal

Muscular contractions. Languor and weakness.

Increases the quantity of milk in nursing

organs.

HERBAL- Rumex is an old Latin word for "lance,"
referring to the shape of the leaves. Crispus
means "curly," also in reference to the leaf shape.
The yellow dock or curly dock is a common British
weed, a member of the buckwheat family. It grows
abundantly throughout North America.
The common yellow dock includes the species
Rumex occidentalis, Rumex venosus, Rumex
obtusifolius and Rumex sangineus, which are
used interchangeably with Rumex crispus.
The common dock of fields and roadsides,
Rumex obtusifolia has awell deserved reputation
among children as the best antidote to the nettle's
sting. Rumex crispus, according to Joslin, was
used by herbalists internally and externally for
the cure of scabies.
Yellow dock has been used for hundreds of
years for its astringent properties, treating a
variety of skin problems, including boils, rashes,
blemishes and burns. Topically, the crushed
leaf of yellow dock can soothe the stings from
nettle plants.
It can also be added to a tooth powder for
spongy gums, and to a gargle for laryngitis.
Salves, poultices or compresses of this herb
have been used for eczema, hives, itchy skin,
scabies and ringworm.

Yellow dock is valued today as one of the

Yellow dock has also been known to help

P. P. Wells related the case of Mrs. X., who
had eight miscarriages all in the early months
of pregnancy. Each miscarriage was attended
with a severe dry, shaking, spasmodic cough in
violent attacks. This was regarded as the cause
of the miscarriages.
At the beginning of the ninth pregnancy she
came under homeopathic treatment. The cough
came on very dry, harsh, loud, shaking, worse
at night, preventing sleep, excited instantly by
pressure on the trachea. Rumx. 30c promptly
relieved.
Wells also cured with Rumx. 200c a cough
in a man that began with tickling behind top of
sternum, sometimes in paroxysms lasting for
five to ten minutes.
Joslin pointed out the left chest had more verified symptoms than any other region. Conditions
are worse lying on left side, better lying on right

HERBAL- The common rue is a native of southern
Europe. Teste noted that it was formerly in great
repute in medicine for epilepsy, hysteria, hydrophobia and weakness of sight from excessive reading.
Ozaena, nosebleed, foul gumboils, flatulent
colic, and inertia of the bowels have been cured
with it empirically.
Teste added that Ruta graveolens was supposed to be a kind of universal antidote, "Even
in our own time the Roman ladies imagine that
the most odoriferous flowers may be left in their
rooms without the least danger provided a bush
of garden rue be amongst them."
Practitioners have perhaps been deterred from
employing it by the symptoms of acrid-narcotic
poisoning induced by an overdose.
It is noted, in The Treasury of Botany, that
locally applied rue is a powerful irritant and one
species, Ruta montana, is dangerous to handle
even with gloves

HOMEOPATHIC - Sabadilla first appears in homeopathic literature as one of Stapf's additions;
Hahnemann was one of the provers. Stapf's

Medica Pura. Stapf said that the plant was first
described by Monades around the year 1572. At
first, it was almost exclusively used for destroying
lice and worms in putrid ulcers and the intestines.
Sabadilla has affinities for the mucus membranes of the nose, lachrymal glands, anus,
digestive tract, and the nerves. Coryza and
symptoms like hay fever. Allergies. Chilliness,
sensitive to cold.

pains in bones. Formication. Worms. Reflex

trembling or catalepsy. Children's diarrhea with
constant cutting pains.

COMMENTS - In his book, Saw Palmetto, Hale
put together most of the available knowledge
regarding this plant. It is a dwarf palm with a
creeping (or leaning), branching stem, the edges
of leaf and petioles serrate, roots fibrous, large,
half exposed.
The fruit, so-called "berry." is a one-seeded
dupe about the size of an olive, dark purple when
ripe, and ripening in October and November.
The fruit is richer in sugar than sugar cane and
contains two oils, one volatile and one fixed.
The volatile oil is considered to possess the
most characteristic properties of the medicine.
Hale described it as "yellow," but he quoted
John Uri Lloyd of Cincinnati, as writing to him,
"The principal constituent is a volatile oil. This oil
possesses a deep green color." And he goes on
to say that the color is not due to chlorophyll nor
to the copper of the form used in condensing it.

Sabat serrutata
This agrees with Estep's contention that the
preparation of Saba! should be dark-green or
grass-green. The preparation Estep used was
a fluid extract prepared by Burrough Brothers of
Baltimore from the "fresh green berries." Hale
directs that the fresh ripe berries should be used.
Hale's tincture was of fresh ripe berries and
seeds, all crushed and macerated in 90 percent
alcohol for fourteen days and decanted. He noted
that the fluid extract was "probably four times
stronger than the tincture."
C. S. Estep used a dark-green fluid extract
that was made from the fresh green berries and
as "almost as green as grass and has an oily
surface." He made his dilutions from this. Other
preparations disappointed him.
Oil can be prepared from the expressed juice
of the fruit by allowing it to stand a few days.
Saccharated oil is one part of the oil to seven
parts of cane sugar. Malted Saba! is one part of
the oil to seven of Maltine. Aqua Olei Saba!, for
use as a spray, is a preparation suggested by
Hale made by triturating 15 drops of the oil with
Mag-c. 3j., gradually adding a pint of distilled
water and decanting.
The preparation used by Dr. Mullin's prover
was made by Boericke and Tafel. All are agreed
that preparations of the dried fruit and of the
root-bark do not possess the curative powers
of the remedy.
While on a trip through the wilds of Florida,
Hale observed the great fattening properties of
the berries on animals. During summer, food is
scanty and. the wild animals become very thin,
but as 'soon as the palmetto fruit ripens they
improve rapidly. In a few weeks have put on so
much fat that they become easy prey. This fat,
said Hale, "consists principally of olein and will
not make lard."

joints, serous membranes and heels.

SACCHARINUM
(Saccharin)
PHARMACY - sacchin. Saccharinum. Saccharin. Benzoic sulphinide. Saccharine. Artificial
sweetener. Planets: Jupiter. Historical dose:
All potencies.
CLINICAL - Allergies. Bladder, cancer. Bladder,
tumors. Headaches. Hypoglycemia. Insomnia.
HOMEOPATHIC- This substance is a derivative of
benzoic acid, and is made synthetically from coaltar. It is a white powder, readily soluble in warm
water, but to only a slight extent in cold water.
Saccharin is the foundation for many lowcalorie and sugar-free products and is used in
table top sweeteners, baked goods, jams, chewing gum, canned fruit, candy, dessert toppings
and salad dressings.
Saccharin is about 300 times as sweet as
sucrose, but has an unpleasant bitter or metallic aftertaste, especially at high concentrations.
Saccharin goes directly through the human
digestive system without being digested. It does
not affect blood insulin levels, and has effectively
no food value.
Saccharin is not recommend for children with
"sulfa" allergies, and has been linked to shortterm problems with infant muscle tone, "lazy"
eye, irritability, and insomnia.
Saccharin has been implicated in the development of photosensitive skin eruptions
in humans, and as a hypoglycemic agent in
animals. Increased incidences of bladder cancer
and tumors have been found in toxicity studies.
RELATIONS- Compare: (1) Aspart., Sac-alb.
REFERENCES - Mu~h~

HOMEOPATHIC - According to Hering, a large
proportion of chronic diseases of women and
children are developed by using too much sugar.
Like so many other articles of diet, Sugar may
be a poison and a medicine as well as a food .
Sugar preserves food , as salt does, and both
sugar and salt have produced scurvy.
Cases of scurvy, rickets in bottle-fed chil·
dren have been traced to excess of sugar in their
food and the exclusion of sugar from the dietary
of the gouty, rheumatic and the diabetic, shows
the pathogenetic power it is credited. Acidity of
the stomach and itching at the anus are common
effects of taking too much sugar.
Sugar is an antiseptic. Combats infection
and putrefaction. It has a solvent action on fibrin
and stimulates secretion by the osmotic changes
·induced, thus rinsing out the wound with serum
from within outward, favoring healing. Leg ulcers.
Sensitive to pain or not sensitive to pain at
all. Fainting on seeing blood. Fainting from pain.
Fainting from a blood puncture. Fainting spells.
Plethora. Weakness, lack of energy. Sudden
weakness, ameliorated by eating. Weakness
after sweets.

SALOL

PHARMACY-salm-1. Salmonella typhi. Salmonella
nosode. Bacteria. Planets: Moon. Historical
dose: All potencies.
CLINICAL-Cholecystitis. Dehydration. Diarrhea.
Enteritis. Fever. Food poisoning. Gastroenteritis. Heartburn. Nausea. Pancreatitis. Salmonellosis. Typhoid fever. Ulcers. Vomiting.
HOMEOPATHIC-The attenuations of this bacteria
nosode are prepared from washings of a culture of
Salmonella typhi. Disease-causing salmonellae
have recently been re-classified into a single species, Salmonella enterica, which has numerous
strains. Salmonella typhi is a well-known strain
that causes typhoid fever.
Other salmonellae are frequent causes of
food-borne illness,especially in poultry and raw
eggs, and more generally from food that has been
cooked or frozen, and not eaten straight away.
The acute symptoms of salmonella gastroenteritis include the sudden onset of nausea,
abdominal cramping, and bloody diarrhea
with mucus. The onset of symptoms usually
occurs within 6 to 72 hours after the ingestion
of the bacteria.
Salmonella infections usually resolve in
five to seven days, and often require no treatment, unless the patient becomes severely
dehydrated or the infection spreads from the
intestines. Persons with severe diarrhea may
require rehydration,often with intravenous fluids.
Some salmonella bacteria have become resistant to antibiotics, however, and this has occurred
possibly as a result of the use of antibiotics to
promote the growth of feed animals.
Confusion and mental vagueness, e.g. in
cerebral degeneration. Highly febrile illnesses.
Enteritis. History of intestinal infections or acute
inflammatory fever. Chronic cholangitis and
cholecystitis. Cholelithiasis. Duodenal and gastric
ulcer. Chronic pancreatitis.

COMMENTS - The leaves of Sambucus nigra
have an unpleasant odor when bruised, which
is supposed to be offensive to most insects. A
decoction of the leaves is sometimes used by
gardeners to keep caterpillars off delicate plants.
Green noted that sheep that have the rot can
be cured by letting them eat the bark and young
leaves of Samb. Herbalists use the inner bark,
as well as the leaves, to make an ointment. The
flowers serve for fomentations or are made into
a medicinal tea. According to the Treasury of
Botany, the berries are the principal ingredient
in elderberry wine.
Millspaugh said that the bark contains vibumic
acid, which is identical with valerianic acid. This
no doubt accounts for the odor and suggests
a relationship in action between sambucus,
valerian and the viburnum.
Nash once relieved with Samb. 200c a very
bad case of asthma in an old woman, who had
suffocative attacks. The relief was accompanied
by a profuse flow of urine, which carried off a
large amount of dropsical effusion in her legs
and abdomen.
Severe croup, whooping cough, bronchitis,
and asthma. Infants with chronic snuffles
(Thuj., after vaccinations). Suffocating attacks
(lp.). Tendency for attacks to recur. Croupy attack
"passes off but is again repeated." Spasms in
the throat. Severe coughing with mucus. Thick,
white, upper respiratory mucus that suffocates
and gags the person (Ant-I.)
Patient can wake up in the middle of the night,
grab at their throat, face turns blue. Waking with
a spasm where the oxygen gets cut off (Cup.).
Worse about midnight or after midnight, worse
2:00. a.m. to 3:00 a.m. Worse dry, cold air.

from getting septic.

Sandalwood oil must be aged at least sixmonths

HERBAL - The bloodroot is commonly found
throughout the United States and Canada, and is
the sole representative of the genus Sanguinaria
of the Papaveraceae. It is herbaceous, has a
thick, branching root stock, which creeps along
underground.

5

Sanguinaria canadensis

In early spring, it sends up from the ends of
the little side branches a single long-stalked leaf
and another stalk bearing a solitary flower. The
leaf is wrapped around the flower bud when it
rises from the ground and is bluntly five to ninelobed, roundish at first, but later kidney-shaped.
The Treasury of Botany noted that Native
Americans used the orange-colored juice of the
root for smearing their bodies and for staining
various domestic articles. The plant had also been
successfully used by American and French dyers.

Sanguinaria canadensis
"Burning" is one of the leading notes of the
remedy and is found in many different parts.
Winterbum published a case illustrating this
indication in the region of the stomach. Mr. F., 48,
of sanguine-bilious temperament, energetic and
refined, had been ill with pains in the stomach
for several months.
Aclairvoyant had recommended "adecoction of
blood-root and bone-set in tablespoonful doses."
Each dose produced "intense burning pains in
the stomach lasting for hours," and it had to be
discontinued.
Weeks later, Winterbum was consulted and
found Mr. F with burning in his epigastrium with
pressure, worse at night, but coming on soon
after lying down and compelling the patient to
rise. Belching gave no relief. Great appetite, torpid
bowels, an unsatisfactory relief each morning,
leaving a sense of discomfort.
There was a peculiar drawing pain in the
shoulders and arms during sleep, so that when
he woke his fists were tightly clenched and flexed
on the sternal end of his clavicle, lameness and
weariness of the muscles followed.
Sang. 200c, was chosen after careful comparison with Nux-v., Graph. and others. It was
given every night at bedtime. After the first dose,
the symptoms disappeared "like magic," and the
patient was soon well.
Leonard said ·a circumscribed burning in
the chest, commonly followed by heat through
abdomen and diarrhea," is a strong indication
for Sang. in pneumonia conditions.
Sang. also has the circumscribed hectic flush
on the cheeks, as in tuberculosis in which it is
frequently indicated. Flushed face, at times
dark red or livid (Op.). It has the "hopefulness"
of tubercular patients.

SASSAFRAS OFFICINALE

SAUERKRAUT

PHARMACY- sass. Sassafras officinale. Sassafras
albidum. Saxifras.Ague tree. Cinnamon wood. Saloop.N.O. Lauraceae. Planets:Venus. Historical
dose: Tincture and all potencies.
CLINICAL - Bladder, problems. Bruises. Cystitis.
Dermatitis. Dropsy. Eye, disorders. Fever.
Gangrene. Gleet. Gonorrhea. Gout. Insect bites.
Kidney, diseases. Ophthalmia. Rheumatism.
Rhus poisoning. Scurvy. Skin diseases. Sprains.
Stings. Syphilis. Wens.
HERBAL-Sassafras is awarm, aromatic stimulant,
alterative, diaphoretic, and diuretic. It has been
used in diseases of the kidneys and bladder.
Medicinally, sassafras has been applied to
insect bites and stings to relieve symptoms. The
oil is said to relieve the pain caused by menstrual
obstructions, and pain following parturition, in
doses of 5 to 10 drops on sugar, the same dose
having been found useful in gleetand gonorrhea.
Dr. Shelby of Huntsville stated that it would
both prevent and remove the injurious effects of
tobacco. The mucilage of the pith (2 drachms to
1 pint of water) is used as a local application in
acute ophthalmia, and is a demulcent drink in
disorders of chest, bowels, kidneys, and bladder.
Externally, as a rubefacient, in painful swellings, sprains, bruises, rheumatism, etc., and is
said to check the progress of gangrene.
An infusion of the bark administered internally
and applied externally is reputed an excellent
treatment for rhus poisoning. Dr. King has also
used it internally in gonorrhea and gleet, 5 to 10
drops on sugar, 3 times a day.
The leaves could be made into teas and
poultices, while the root bark was either chipped
or crushed and then steeped in boiling water.
One ounce of bark to one pint of water, taken
in doses of a wineglassful as often as needed
to reduce fevers.
COMMENTS - One teaspoon of the pure oil is
enough to cause vomiting, dilated pupils, stupor,
collapse and even death! Sassafras formerly
was used as a flavoring in root beer. Sassafras
oil and safrole have been banned for use as a
drug and as flavors and food additives by the
FDA because of their carcinogenic potential.
REFERENCES - Murphy.

PHARMACY - Sauerkraut. Brassica oleracea. Sauerkraut directly translated means "sour cabbage".
Planets: Jupiter. Historical dose: All potencies.
CLINICAL - Acid reflux. Acidity. Allergies. Bowel,
flora. Cancer. Candida. Celiac, disease. Cholesterol. Colds. Colitis. Constipation.Crohn'sdisease.
Dehydration. Diarrhea. Dysentery. Fatigue.
Flatus. Food, poisoning. Heartburn. Indigestion.
Infections. Influenza. Irritable bowel syndrome.
Scurvy. Stomach, disorders.
HERBAL- Historical evidence suggests laborers on
the Great Wall of China consumed a version of the
pickled cabbage dish 2,000 years ago. Traditional
Chinese has long prescribed sauerkraut juice as a
home remedy for many common ailments.
Sauerkraut is believed to have been introduced
to Europe in its present form 1,000 years later by
Genghis Khan after plundering China. The Tartars
took it in their saddlebags to Europe. There it took
root mosUy in Eastern European and Germanic
cuisines, but also in countries such as France.
The Roman army traveled with barrels of sauerkraut, using it to prevent intestinal infections among
the troops during long excursions.
The benefits of sauerkraut and sauerkraut juice
have been recognized for generations.In some families of southern Germany, the children are fed raw
sauerkraut twice weekly to support their intestines.
Sauerkraut combines the health benefits offered
by all cruciferous vegetables with the probiotic
advantages derived from the fermentation process.
Sauerkraut is finely cut cabbage that has been
fermented by various lactic acid bacteria, induding
Leuconostoc, Lactobacillus, and Pediococcus.lthas
a long shelf-life and a distinctive sour flavor, both
of which result from the lactic acid that forms when
the bacteria ferment the sugars in the cabbage.
Sauerkraut also contains live lactobacilli and
beneficial microbes and is rich in enzymes, if unpasteurized and uncooked,. The fiber and supply
of probiotics improve digestion and promote the
growth of healthy bowel flora, protecting against
many diseases of the digestive tract.
Nutritive and bowel tonic. Antioxidants. AntiInflammatory. Digestive aid.

Fermented foods improve digestion, restore

However, most commercially sold sauerkraut

There are only two ingredients in traditional
sauerkraut: shredded cabbage and salt. The
cabbage is tossed with copious amounts of salt
and then tightly packed into a crock or airtight
jar. The salty conditions promote beneficial acid
forming bacteria, which convert the natural sugars
in the cabbage into lactic and acetic acid, which
will preserve the cabbage and give it a tang.
If using a traditional crock, the sauerkraut must
periodically be skimmed to remove natural scum;
once cured, the dish can be canned and kept
for up to several years.To reap the benefits of
sauerkraut, it's not necessary to eat a lot of it.

Sea buckthorn, fruit oil- Fruit oil is prepared

into another bowl. Thirty drops are administrated

Sea buckthorn, fruit syrup. By mixing half a
liter of juice with half a liter of honey, fruit syrup
is obtained. After homogenization the syrup is
kept in the fridge. The syrup treatment consists
of taking from four to six spoons a day.

for 10 minutes. It is then left to cool down and
after that it gets strained. The remaining twigs
are burnt and the resulting ash is mixed with
the mixture based on vinegar obtained before.

active substances. It is used as a source of betacarotene. This oil has a natural taste and aroma.

buckthorn seeds over which 500g of honey is

Sea buckthorn, tea · Sea buckthorn tea can

The tea is recommended in cases of diarrhea,

is obtained by putting two spoons of mashed

the pot covered for about 30 minutes its content
is passed through a sieve.

HOMEOPATHIC - Rye and grasses are apt to be

and when grown on damp, ill-drained lands. If
breeding cows are turned on pastures where
infected grasses grow, they are very liable to
drop their calves. Ergot has been known to
hasten childbirth from remote times.
Secale's other actions have been, for the
most part, learned from the terrible epidemics of
"ergotism "which have occasionally devastated
districts in which rye infected with ergot has been
ground into nour and eaten by the population.
Death takes places in convulsions, from
gangrene and consequent exhaustion, or from

diarrhea.
Many who escape immediate death are reduced to a cachectic state from which they never
recover, are paralyzed, have limbs distorted and

HERBAL-Senega is one of the sources of Saponin.
It has a nauseous taste and leaves a scraping
sensation in the throat. It is in disorders of the
chest, eyes and bladder that homeopaths have
found it of most service and the extensive provings have supplied excellent data for prescribing.
Teste reported that Seneg. was introduced to
medical practice by Dr.Tennant of Virginia,who was
led to test its properties through hearing that the Native Americans used it as an antidote to snakebites
as it relieved the symptoms of snakes' venom.
Tennant concluded that it might also relieve
dyspnea, cough and hemoptysis arising from
other causes and gave it with success in cases
of pneumonia, pleurisy and hydrothorax.
Other old-school practitioners used it as an
expectorant in chronic respiratory catarrh, acute
tuberculosis, rheumatic fever, dropsies incipient
cataract, croup. It is regarded as "a stimulant,diaphoretic and expectorant in chronic bronchitis.'

SEROTONIN
PHARMACY - serot. Serotonin. A brain neurotransmitter. Planets: Moon. Historical dose:
All potencies.
CLINICAL - Alcoholism. Alzheimer's disease.
Anxiety. Autism. Bipolar disorder. Bulimia.
Clumsiness. Compulsive disorders. Depression. Drowsiness. Edema. Insomnia. Learning,
disorders. Migraine. Nightmares. Palpitations.
Restlessness. Schizophrenia. Suicidal. Twitch·
ing. Vertigo.
HOMEOPATHIC- Serotonin is a neurotransmitter
produced in the brain known to influence the
functioning of the cardiovascular, renal,immune,
and gastrointestinal systems. In the nervous
system, serotonin is believed to play an important
role in the regulation of mood, sleep, vomiting,
sexuality and appetite.
Serotonin has been thought to play a part in
many disorders, notably as part ofthe biochemistry of depression, migraine, bipolar disorder and
anxiety. Recent research suggests that serotonin
also plays an important role in liver regeneration.
It is well known that abnormal serotonin levels
can cause various types of sexual dysfunction
such as anorgasmia, erectile dysfunction,
and diminished libido. Serotonin also causes
problems such as insomnia, depression, obesity, eating disorders,premenstrual syndrome,
panic attacks, alcoholism, anxiety disorders,
and bulimia.

5

Serotonin

Serotonin, at increasing levels, stimulates
nervous tension, drowsiness, heart palpitations,
water retention and inability to concentrate and
perform.
Any disruption in the synthesis, metabolism or
uptake of this neurotransmitter has been found
to be responsible for certain manifestations
of schizophrenia, depression, compulsive
disorders and learning problems. Increase
in brain levels of either of neurotransmitter,
serotonin, produces a craving for alcohol,
anger, or anxiety, especially for those who have

Serrapeptase, technically called Serratia
Peptidase, is a proteolytic enzyme, which means
that it chops up or digests protein. It is produced
by bacteria in the gut of silkworms and is used
to digest their cocoons.
When this enzyme is isolated and coated in

Serrapeptase has been used in Europe and

Shiitake, fresh: When shopping for fresh shiitakes, avoid those grown in a sawdust medium and
opt for log-grown mushrooms. You can recognize a
shiitake grown on outdoor logs: it has a dark brown

Sawdust-medium shiitakes have flat tops. are

mushrooms.Shiitakes never come in contact 11/ith

their chewiness. Sauteing is the most common
ways of eating shiitakes. One of the techniques
for sauteing shiitakes is maintaining the sound of
constant sizzling while they're in the pan, which
means you're cooking them over lively heat. You
wantthe shiitakes to develop a brown. crisp outside,
which will boost their flavor..
Shiitake, dried: When shopping for dried shiitakes, look for mushrooms with thick brown caps
ridged with white. Before using dried shiitakes in
a recipe, even if irs a soup or a stew, ifs best to
rehydrate them in hot water. The stems tend to be
woody, so trim them off and discard after soaking.
To store dried shiitakes for a short time (a month
or less), seal the mushrooms in an airtight container
or ziptop bag and store in a cool, dark place.
For long-term storage, seal the dried mushrooms
in heavy-duty freezer bags and put them in the
freezer where they'll keep indefinitely.
Shiitake, powder: Add 1 - 2 teaspoons to dishes.
sauces, smoothies or infuse in a tea.

PHARMACY-Eleutherococcus senticosus. Siberian
ginseng.Russian Ginseng.Planets: Moon. Historical dose: All potencies.
CLINICAL - Arthritis. Autoimmune disorders. Bronchitis. Cancer. Chemotherapy, illness. Colds.
Debility. Diabetes. Emaciation. Eye, disorders.
Fatigue. Fevers. Fibromyalgia. Glaucoma. Hair,
loss. Herpes.Immune, problems. Infections.Liver,
disease. Menopause. Nausea. Poisoning. Radiation, illness. Stress. Toxicity. Tumors. Vomiting.
Weight, loss. Weakness.
HERBAL· Siberian Ginseng or Eleuthero has been
used in China for 2000 years as a folk remedy for
bronchitis, heart ailments, and rheumatism. and
as a tonic to restore vigor, improve general health,
restore memory, promote healthy appetite, and
increase stamina.
In Chinese medicine, it was used to prevent
respiratory tract infections as well as colds and
flu. It was also believed to provide energy and
vitality. In Russia, Siberian Ginseng was originally
used by people in the Siberian Taiga region to
increase performance and quality of life and to
decrease infections.
Regular use is said to restore vigor, improve
the memory and increase longevity. It has been
used during convalescence and in the treatment
of menopausal problems, geriatric debility, physical and mental stress.
Adaptogen. Siberian Ginseng has shown
anti-viral and anti-cancer properties.
Eleuthero is often recommended as a general
tonic to revitalize people who are fatigued.

1866

Siberian ginseng
Because it enhances immunity and helps the
body deal with stress eleuthero is frequently
included in nutritional support programs for
people with fibromyalgia, arthritis and other
autoimmune disorders.
Adrenal glands • Siberian ginseng restores
overstressed adrenal glands, working wonders
for people who are chronically stressed. The
adrenal glands have a big impact on sexual
health because of the their role in producing a
variety of hormone that regulate many physical
responses. Tonic herbs such as eleuthero help
to prevent "adrenal burnout" caused by ongoing
physical or mental challenges.
Anti-aging • One study found that elderly
people who took Siberian ginseng improved
mental health and social functioning after 4weeks
of therapy, compared to those who took placebo.
Anti-inflammatory • Other uses for Siberian
ginseng are for chronic inflammatory conditions
and traditionally for functional weakness.
Cancer· Other research with cancer patients
has linked Siberian ginseng with improved
healing and recovery times, increased weight
gain, and improved immune functions. Siberian
Ginseng has been shown to have preventive effects against breast cancer, stomach cancer, oral
cavity cancer, skin melanoma and ovarian cancer.
Chemotherapy· Siberian ginseng is now used
in the support of cancer patients undergoing
chemotherapy. Studies have shown that Siberian
ginseng, when administered to patients, drastically reduces the side effects of chemotherapy
(e.g., nausea, weakness, fatigue, diuiness, and
loss of appetite).
Colds and flu • Some double-blind studies
have found that a specific product containing
Siberian ginseng and andrographis reduced the
severity and length of colds, when taken with 72
hours of symptoms starting. Researchers don't
know whether Siberian ginseng was responsible,
or whether it was·andrographis or the combination
of the two herbs.
Detox • Another way that eleuthero reduces
stress on the body is to combat harmful toxins.
Siberian Ginseng has shown a protective effect
in animal studies, against chemicals such as
ethanol, sodium barbital, tetanus toxoid, and
chemotherapeutic agents. It can also reduce
the side effects of radiation exposure.

Siberian ginseng

Energy- Siberian Ginseng has been shown to
enhance mental acuity and physical endurance
without the letdown that comes with caffeinated
products. Research has shown that eleuthero
improves the use of oxygen by the exercising
muscle. This means that a person is able to
maintain aerobic exercise longer and recovery
from workouts is much quicker.
Eyes - Several studies were conducted to
evaluate the effects of Siberian Ginseng on
eye conditions and color distinction. One study
evaluated the pre and post-operative effects of
eleuthero extract on male or female patients
suffering from primary glaucoma and eye burns.
Beneficial effects were noted in both treatments.
Siberian Ginseng was also found beneficial in
cases of myopia treatment.
Herpes- One double-blind study of 93 people
with herpes simplex virus type 2, which can cause
genital herpes, found that taking Siberian ginseng
reduced the number of outbreaks. Outbreaks
that did happen were less severe and didn't last
as long. Talk to your doctor about whether use
Siberian ginseng as a supplement to prevent
herpes outbreaks is right for you.
Immunity - Evidence is also mounting that
Siberian ginseng enhances and supports the
immune response. Eleuthero may be useful as a
preventive measure during cold and flu season.
Healthy people who took Siberian ginseng for
4 weeks had more T-cells, which may indicate
strengthening of the immune systems. It may help
the long-term management of various diseases
of the immune system, including HIV infection,
chronic fatigue syndrome, and autoimmune
illnesses such as lupus.
Mental health - Siberian ginseng boosts
concentration and focus without the letdown than
comes from stimulants like caffeine. Siberian
ginseng is often .used to maintain or restore
mental alertness. But there haven't been enough
scientific studies to know whether it really works.
One preliminary study found that middle-aged volunteers who took Siberian ginseng improved their
memory compared to those who took placebo.
Physical - Although Siberian ginseng is frequently suggested to improve physical stamina
and increase muscle strength, studies have
shown only mixed results.

s

Siberian ginseng

Radiation- After the Chernobyl accident, many
Russian citizens were given Siberian Ginseng
to counteract the effects of radiation. Siberian
ginseng is also used in the support of cancer
patients undergoing radiation therapy. Studies
have shown that Siberian ginseng drastically
reduces the side effects of radiation therapy
(e.g., nausea, weakness, fatigue, dizziness, and
loss of appetite).
Sports- Siberian ginseng's ability to increase
stamina and endurance led Soviet Olympic athletes to use it to enhance their training. Explorers,
divers, sailors, and miners used it to prevent
stress-related illness. By boosting recovery
following hard workouts, Siberian ginseng may
also downgrade athletes' chances of overtraining.
Extracts of Siberian ginseng appear to have the
ability to prevent immune suppression in vigorously training athletes.
Weight loss - Siberian ginseng does not
promote weight loss directly, when you feel more
energetic and less stressed, you're more likely to
stick to your new exercise and diet routine. Diets
with severe calorie restrictions, can be draining
on energy levels and raise stress levels. This
elevates stress hormones like cortisol that make
weight loss more difficult.
COMMENTS - In traditional Chinese medicine,
eleuthero is considered good for vital energy (qil
chi), used for sleeplessness with many dreams,
lower back or kidney pain, deficiency of yang in the
kidney or spleen, lack of appetite, and to enhance
overall resistance to disease or stress. For treating
arthritis and making muscles and bones strong, one
prescription mixes wu-jia-pi with sweet rice wine.
Eleuthero is a great tonic in times of fatigue and
debility,declining capacity for work or concentration,
and during convalescence.
Siberian ginseng is available as liquid extracts,
solid extracts, powders, capsules, and tablets, and
as dried or cut root for tea. Successful studies that
were done with an alcohol extract. Siberian ginseng
is also available in a tablet, capsule, or tea form.
Decoction: 1-2 teaspoons of dry herb per cup
of water; or liquid extract: 10-20 drops 1-4 times
per day. For chronic conditions, such as fatigue or
stress, Siberian ginseng can be taken for 3 months,
followed by 3 - 4 weeks off.
RELATIONS- Ginseng. Cordyceps. Gynostemma.
REFERENCES - Murphy.

Schussler. who was a homeopath before he
was a biochemist, noted that silicic acid, from the
tissue remedy point of view, is a constituent of the
cells of the connective tissue or the epidermis,
the hair and the nails.
It may be used if asuppurative center is formed
either in the connective tissue or in a portion of the
skin. These cells are thereby enabled to throw off
inimical substances (the pus). ln consequences,
the pus is either absorbed by the lymphatics or it
is cast out. In the latter case there is a breaking
open of the suppurative center. Sil. may also
cause an effusion of blood in any tissue to be
absorbed through the lymphatics.
Teste put Sil. in his Puis. group of remedies.
the other members of it being Calc., Hep.,
Graph., and Phos. According to Teste, Sil. is the
"chronic" of Puis.
Sil. corresponds to the chronic form of such
diseases as Puis. cures when acute, including
rush of blood to the head, especially to the right
temple and vertex, headache every day, photophobia, lachrymation ,loss of taste. and aversion
to fat food with rancid or oily taste in the mouth.
The symptoms of Sil. differ from those of Puis.,
being more constant, more deep-seated and
lasting longer. For instance, the mucus secretions of Puis. easily become purulent under the
action of Sil.
Sil. is useful for chronic arthritic or rheumatic
affections as it forms a soluble combination (sodium silicate) with the soda of the urate of soda.
this combination is then absorbed and removed
through the lymphatics. For the same reason it
may also be used in kidney gravel.

Indians in treating snake bites, by bruising and
moistening the roots and applying to the wound.'
The symptoms of the snake bites cured with

hot and dry, face dark red. The leg and foot are

COMMENTS - Dr. W. U. Reed stated 'We have
growing in our woods and fields a small plant,
which I believe to be a specific for the treatment
of persons or animals bitten by the rattlesnake.
From my own experience and observation in the
use of this remedy, I believe it to be a positive cure
in all cases if exhibited in any reasonable time.
"I have never known it to fail in a single instance,
even where the alcoholic treatment and many
other kinds had failed. I am not aware of its ever
having been used as a medicine by the profession
and, so far as I know, I am the first to prepare
and use it in the form of a tincture."
Dr. Reed gave these cases: "(1) Bessie A.,
aged six years, while playing in the yard on a
farm, some twelve miles in the country, was bitten
in the hand by a rattlesnake which was killed a
moment after by the mother of the little girl who
was attracted by the screams of the child.
"Sixteen hours after Iarrived, everything having
been done in the meantime that had ever been
heard of by the parents, even to applying a poultice the wound with entrails of a black chicken.
"The little sufferer was indeed, an object of
pity. The hand and arm were swollen almost to
bursting, the swelling extending to the shoulder
and spine, being of a blush black color as if
dreadfully bruised. This discoloration extended
over the back to the hips. Skin hot and dry, face
nushed, pulse quick and hard. Child unconscious.
"I felt that the case was hopeless. But, through
the earnest entreaties of the mother, I proceeded
to do what I could. Saturating a piece of cotton
with the tincture I had prepared, I bound it on the
wound, then dropping twelve drops in a glass
of water I directed that a teaspoonful be given
every hour, the compress to be renewed every
hour also, until my return.
"I confess I had little hope of seeing my little
patient alive again but on my return the following
day I was much rejoiced to find a decided change
for the better in the condition of the little sufferer.
The swelling was not nearly so tense, the fever
had subsided, the delirium gone and the danger
seemed past. The treatment was continued and
a speedy and permanent recovery followed.
"(2) Burt Whitten, aged ten, while out in a marsh
with a number of older boys gathering huckleberries, was bitten in the right ankle by a rattler.

from four provers and from Reichenbach's
experiences from hypersensitives. The common
effects of strong sunlight, such as sneezing,
freckling and sunstroke, may be added to the list
Dr. Thayer, in 1893 in southern California,
wrote a paper on sunlight for a homeopathic
journal. He described how to "Concentrate the
sun rays to a diseased part until slightly burned
or charred and then wait until it heals and then
repeat the procedure."
He claimed to have cured all kinds of cancers,
removed birthmarks, tattoos, warts, sebaceous
cysts, ulcers, varicose veins and all other types
of benign growths. "Unlike other caustics, it can
be applied upon the most delicate of tissues and
it causes only slight irritation and most heal with
only the slightest scar."
Dr. Thayer coined the term "solar cauterization." A magnifying glass was used and the
sunbeam was focused right on the skin cancer,
until a burning sensation was felt, then stopped.
This would be repeated once or twice aday.After
a week or ten days the melanoma would fall off
and it would heal without a scar.
Thayer had a whole practice based on the mag·
nifying glass and focusing the sunlight in 1893
and very few homeopaths used his methods.
Dr. Foubister revived interest in Sol in itspotentized form as an antidote for radiation poisoning
from radiation therapy with cancer patients.

respiratory paralysis with accumulations of mucus
